content_list.content_text: The Hollywood Western began to decline at the end of the 1950s. The enemy of the communities forging a new life for themselves on the great frontier was no longer the gunslinger dressed in black or the marauding Indian, but the specter of television, which offered audiences cheap series such as Gunsmoke and Bonanza. The genre would still have its swan song, however. It would be saved by the most un-Western place in the world - Europe.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from Once Upon a Time in the West
information.contentText: Director Sergio Leone intended for the three leads of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, Clint Eastwood, Lee Van Cleef and Eli Wallach, to make a brief cameo in the segment at the very beginning of the film, but since Eastwood was unavailable during the shooting of Once Upon a Time in the West, the idea was eventually shelved.

content_list.content_text: Film production in Europe gained momentum in the decade following the end of World War II, and Hollywood was the obvious model for producers to follow. Michael Carreras (1927-1994), of Hammer Film Productions, made the first Spaghetti Western, Tierra brutal (The Savage Guns, 1961), an English-language Anglo-Spanish coproduction.

Except, however, for the English-speaking actors who sometimes appeared in these films, the new genre's language of choice was Italian. The first great Spaghetti Westerns were driven by a desire to reinvent the American Western and the Japanese samurai film. Sergio Leone (1929-1989) loosely based his Per un pugno di dollari (A Fistful of Dollars, 1964) on Yojimbo (1961), by Akira Kurosawa (1910-1998).

information.contentTitle: Scenes from The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
information.contentText:
The score was composed by Leone's frequent collaborator Ennio Morricone, whose distinctive original compositions, featuring gunshots, whistling (by John O'Neill) and yodeling, permeate the film. The main theme, which resembles the howl of a coyote (and blends with the howl of a real coyote in the first scene after the opening credits), is a two-note melody that recurs as a frequent motif and is used for the three main characters. A different musical instrument was used for each: flute for Blondie, ocarina for Angel Eyes and voices for Tuco. The score complements the film's Civil War setting, featuring the mournful ballad La Storia Di Un Soldato (The Story of a Soldier), which is sung by the prisoners of war while Tuco is tortured by Angel Eyes. The film's climax, a Mexican standoff among the three protagonists, begins with the melody of L'estasi dell'oro (The Ecstasy of Gold) and is followed by Il Triello (The Trio). Today the iconic theme is considered one of the greatest film scores of all time.

The main theme, also called "Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo," was a hit in 1968, with the soundtrack album among the best sellers for more than a year, reaching number four on Billboard magazine's pop chart. In popular culture, the American new wave group Wall of Voodoo performed a medley of Ennio Morricone's film themes, including the theme from this film. The only known recording is a live performance on the album The Index Masters. The punk rock band Ramones played this song as the opener on their live album Loco Live, as well as at other shows, until their breakup in 1996. The British heavy metal band Motörhead played the theme as an opener on the 1981 No Sleep 'til Hammersmith tour. The American heavy metal band Metallica has played L'estasi dell'oro as a prelude to its shows since 1985 (except from 1996 to 1998) and, in 2007, recorded an instrumental version for a Morricone tribute compilation. XM Satellite Radio's The Opie & Anthony Show also used L'estasi dell'oro as its opening theme. The song Urban Struggle, by the American punk rock band The Vandals, opens with the main theme. The electronic group Bomb the Bass used the theme from Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo as one of the samples in its 1988 song Beat Dis, along with parts of Tuco's dialogue as he is about to be hanged in the song Throughout The Entire World, the opening track of its 1991 album Unknown Territory. A song by the band Gorillaz is called Clint Eastwood and features references to the actor, with the iconic cry heard in the film's theme.

content_list.content_text: In terms of morality, setting and style, the first film contrasts sharply with traditional Westerns. There are no good characters: the hero, played by Clint Eastwood (b. 1930) - star of the TV show Rawhide -, is a gunslinger driven by personal gain, with only momentary flashes of conscience. Native Americans play no role at all, not even in C'era una volta il West (Once Upon a Time in the West, 1968), which plays with the archetypal setting of westward expansion and its dangers.

content_list.title: The Masterpiece of the Western
content_list.description:
By the mid-1960s, Hollywood had grown tired of Westerns, which were increasingly seen as a relic of another era. Naturally, the films remained essential to understanding the history of cinema, but the times were changing and the genre no longer seemed to have a place in popular culture. Sergio Leone thought otherwise. The Italian director sensed that the dying genre was ripe for reinvention. The lasting influence of his so-called spaghetti Westerns (nicknamed for their Italian locations and their copious use of blood) shows that he was right.

Leone had made a handful of films before inviting the relatively unknown Clint Eastwood to Italy for a remake of Akira Kurosawa's Yojimbo (1961), itself based on Dashiell Hammett's Red Harvest. A Fistful of Dollars (1964) was the first of the iconic Westerns starring the "Man with No Name". Made on a minimal budget, this innovative and refined film became a huge hit, and Leone followed it with For a Few Dollars More (1965), again starring Eastwood as another laconic, anonymous antihero. But the third part of the "Man with No Name" trilogy, The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, is the work that confirmed Leone's reputation as a film legend.

Leone is not terribly interested in plot - in The Good, the Bad and the Ugly he is concerned with purely cinematic elements. He carefully composes every widescreen image as if he were painting a vast landscape; he indulges in extreme close-ups that often reveal little more than a character's eyes. Then there are his radical editing techniques, set to the rhythm of Ennio Morricone's famous score, which places unusual instruments and electric guitars alongside traditional orchestration. Every frame is coated in style the way sweat permanently coats the stars' faces.

The Good, the Bad and the Ugly literally ends on the faces of Eastwood, Wallach and Van Cleef, as the antagonists stage a three-way duel in a cemetery. This scene has become one of the most imitated and parodied in film history. Morricone's hypnotic score builds in intensity while on screen ever-faster cuts move from one face to another, capturing every tense glance, every hand reaching for a gun. Camp, kitsch and exhilarating, the film is the work of a master rewriting the rules of the Western to suit Leone's singular vision.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: Instead, most of the action unfolds in the Southern states, where Mexico and the Latino population play significant roles. Leone's world was violent and propelled by the celebrated music of Ennio Morricone (1928-2020). The director's next film, Per qualche dollaro in più (For a Few Dollars More, 1965), teamed Lee Van Cleef (1925-1989) with Eastwood, who plays a young upstart seeking a bit of moral guidance from a veteran more interested in revenge.

information.contentTitle: Scenes from For a Few Dollars More
information.contentText: Released in the United States in 1967, the film is the second part of director Leone's so-called Dollars Trilogy. Clint Eastwood is the lead in this and the other films, always playing a Man with No Name, the role that made him famous early in his career.

content_list.content_text: Leone was once again helped by Morricone's music, with a central theme that highlights his gift for subtlety and adds emotional weight to the shootout that forms the film's climax. Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo (The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, 1966) cemented Leone's reputation as the master of the Spaghetti Western and Morricone's as the go-to composer for filmmakers in the genre.

quote.quote: If you're going to lose, you'd better lose properly. Whoever double-crosses me and leaves me alive, he understands nothing about me. Nothing!
quote.author: Tuco (Eli Wallach) in The Good, the Bad and the Ugly

content_list.content_text: Other directors would also have their careers defined by the Spaghetti Western. Sergio Corbucci (1926-1990) will be remembered for Django (1966), brutal even by the standards of this subgenre. In contrast to Leone's arid settings, Franco Nero's antihero hunts for his loot in a muddy, rain-soaked landscape, dragging a coffin containing his weapon of choice, a machine gun. Gianfranco Parolini (b. 1930) found success with the Sabata trilogy (1969-1971), starring Western stalwarts such as Lee Van Cleef and Yul Brynner.

information.contentText: The film became very popular in Europe and is considered a cult film in the United States. It is one of the best examples of the Spaghetti Western genre, with a rousing soundtrack, gunfights and a laconic antihero who dragged a coffin around with him. The film's unique look is due to the work of art director Carlo Simi, who had already created characters and sets for Corbucci's previous film, Minnesota Clay, and also frequently worked on Sergio Leone's films. In addition to "Django Shoots First" (1966), Viva Django (1968), "Django the Bastard" and "Django Kill... If You Live, Shoot!", the film had an official sequel called Django 2 - Il grande ritorno (Django Strikes Again), which was released in 1987.

content_list.content_text: The films, full of blackmail and shootouts, are driven by the music of Marcello Giombini (1928-2003). Although it is still a great film, in Lo chiamavano Trinità... (They Call Me Trinity, 1970) by Enzo Barboni (1922-2002), comedy betrays the Spaghetti Western, which had already passed its heyday and become prime material for parody. The genre came to an end with Keoma (1976), but the spirit and style of the Spaghetti Western strongly influenced two generations of filmmakers, from Clint Eastwood (b. 1930) and Sam Raimi (b. 1959) to Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963) and Robert Rodriguez (b. 1968).
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Ian Haydn Smith, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
movies.original_title: Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo
movies.overview: While the Civil War rages between the Union and the Confederacy, three men – a quiet loner, a ruthless hit man and a Mexican bandit – comb the American Southwest in search of a strongbox containing $200,000 in stolen gold.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in the West
movies.overview: A widow whose land and life are in danger as the railroad is getting closer and closer to taking them over. A mysterious harmonica player joins forces with a desperado to protect the woman and her land.

movies.title: Django
movies.overview: A coffin-dragging gunslinger and a half-breed prostitute become embroiled in a bitter feud between a merciless masked clan and a band of Mexican revolutionaries.

movies.title: The Savage Guns
movies.overview: This Western is set in the Mexican valley of Sonora not that far south of the state of Arizona. It's just after the American Civil War, and a former Confederate officer, Mike Summers (Don Taylor) has taken refuge in a small town in the valley. He has married and is hoping to live in peace the rest of his life. Instead, he and his wife and the rest of the town are suffering the depredations of a brutal gunman, Danny Pose (Alex Nicol), and his gang of outlaws. Summers holds off picking up a gun because of his personal vow of non-violence. But the situation deteriorates and a new ally comes into the picture, Steve Fallon (Richard Basehart), a wandering gunslinger who may not be able to handle the bad guys alone.

movies.title: A Fistful of Dollars
movies.overview: The Man With No Name enters the Mexican village of San Miguel in the midst of a power struggle among the three Rojo brothers and sheriff John Baxter. When a regiment of Mexican soldiers bearing gold intended to pay for new weapons is waylaid by the Rojo brothers, the stranger inserts himself into the middle of the long-simmering battle, selling false information to both sides for his own benefit.

movies.title: The Great Silence
movies.overview: A mute gunslinger fights in the defense of a group of outlaws and a vengeful young widow, against a group of ruthless bounty hunters.

movies.title: Duck, You Sucker
movies.overview: At the beginning of the 1913 Mexican Revolution, greedy bandit Juan Miranda and idealist John H. Mallory, an Irish Republican Army explosives expert on the lam from the British, fall in with a band of revolutionaries plotting to strike a national bank. When it turns out that the government has been using the bank as a hiding place for illegally detained political prisoners -- who are freed by the blast -- Miranda becomes a revolutionary hero against his will.
